clue.text: ‘Doctor of Retraction’ gets cross

indicators.note: A retraction is a drawing back, so what has just been built is read back the other way.

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
the little word of the clue taken at face value, two letters

explanation.surface: Someone holding a degree in taking back what they said turns out to be bad-tempered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' is the trap: the sentence offers angry, and the grid wants the verb for getting over a river at a shallow place. The quotation marks are there to sell the fake qualification.
explanation.definitionFit: To ford a stream is to cross it by wading, so 'cross' is the plain verb sense of getting to the other side.

clue.text: Given a fancy coat, delivers bananas

indicators.note: Going bananas is losing your mind, and letters that have lost their minds will not stay in the order printed.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A delivery of bananas made by someone kitted out in a smart new coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like the cargo and is the instruction; 'delivers' looks like the job and is the raw material. Mirrors, teapots and trophies all carry this thin coat over a cheaper metal underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: To silver something is to give it a coating of silver, the fancy coat a plain metal gets to smarten it up.

clue.text: See 18 Across
Drink time – oh, so riotous!

indicators.note: A riot is disorder in the street, and letters called riotous have broken out of their proper order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Drinking hour at a party, and what a wild one it turned out to be.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark makes 'oh, so riotous' sound like a verdict on the evening rather than an instruction. The fodder runs straight through the dash and the comma, which are punctuation to be ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoothie is a thick blended drink of fruit and yoghurt, so 'Drink' names it by category.

clue.text: One subsequently meets earth goddess

blocks.note: a is one, as in a dozen meaning one dozen
then = subsequently, next in time
standard abbreviation, the letter marking the earth wire

explanation.surface: One person arriving later and running into a deity of the soil.
explanation.walkthrough: E for earth comes from household wiring, where the earth terminal carries the letter. The whole difficulty is that 'One subsequently meets' reads as an ordinary sentence and is really three separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Athene is the Greek goddess of wisdom and warfare, Athena in the commoner spelling.

clue.text: Try to sell briars as tuning aids?

blocks.note: a salesman pitches what he is trying to shift
a briar is a smoker's pipe, its bowl cut from the root of the briar shrub

explanation.surface: A trader hawking old smokers' pipes as though they were musical equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the leap between two kinds of pipe: one is filled with tobacco, the other is blown. Choirs use the answer to find a starting note where there is no piano.
explanation.definitionFit: A pitch pipe is a small reed pipe sounded to give singers their note, which is exactly an aid to tuning.

clue.text: Wine, gallons, at parties

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
a rave is an all-night dance party

explanation.surface: Wine ordered by the gallon to keep the parties supplied.
explanation.walkthrough: Rave for a party came in with acid house in the late eighties and has stayed; the setter needs it plural. The two commas are the only sign that one short sentence is doing two jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Graves is the Bordeaux district south of the city and the red and white wine made there, so 'Wine' names it by example.

clue.text: Attempt to extract everything from onion

indicators.note: Extracting is pulling something out of what holds it, so those letters leave the longer word and the rest closes up.

blocks.note: the small mild onion sold in nets
everything = all, and those three letters are the ones pulled out

explanation.surface: A cook having a go at getting every last thing out of an onion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attempt' is a noun here — a go, a try — rather than the verb the sentence dangles in front of you. Shallot is worth stocking: it hides ALL and HALL and is a favourite source of both.
explanation.definitionFit: A shot is one go at a target, and that aiming sense widens out to any single try at anything — a job, a guess, a question.

clue.text: Spread moist leaves out

indicators.note: Spreading something scatters it about, and scattered letters keep no fixed order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: Damp leaves laid out to dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' pulls hard towards foliage and belongs to the definition instead: to leave out is to skip. Only the one damp word is fodder, so the anagram is exactly as long as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To omit something is to leave it out, both verbs sitting in the same third-person form.

clue.text: Top female Republican with manic air enters contest

indicators.note: Mania is frenzy, and letters in a frenzy will not stay in the order they were given.
What enters a thing ends up inside it, so these letters are planted within the other word.

blocks.note: a contest is a match
standard abbreviation
three letters of fodder, jumbled together with the R

explanation.surface: A leading Republican woman with a crazed look about her entering a race.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a political contest and the answer is domestic, the senior woman of a family line. 'Contest' supplies the outer word, which is why the jumble lands in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A matriarch is the woman who heads a family or a tribe, so 'top female' states her position plainly.

clue.text: Department head in charge of exclusive sea food

indicators.note: The head of a word is its top, which in writing means its first letter and nothing else.

blocks.note: the head of Department is the letter it starts with
an officer set over you is in charge of you
sole use of something is exclusive use

explanation.surface: A department boss handed control of a restaurant's exclusive fish line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like the person running the department and asks for one letter of the word instead. Dover sole is the flatfish landed off the Kent coast and named for the port, a British restaurant fixture.
explanation.definitionFit: Dover sole is a flatfish sold and eaten as food from the sea, so the definition names the dish by its category.

clue.text: Old Man Time’s desire

blocks.note: cove is dated British slang for a fellow, which is why the clue calls it old
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: What Old Man Time himself wants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desire' is a noun in the sentence and a verb in the grid, and that switch of part of speech is what hides the join. Old Man Time is the hooded figure with the scythe, which is why the capitals look natural.
explanation.definitionFit: To covet is to desire something, usually somebody else's — the verb of the tenth commandment.

clue.text: Administrative division or dividing branch

indicators.note: Something dividing a word comes down in the middle of it and splits it in two.

blocks.note: a bough is a main branch of a tree
the clue's own little word, dropped in whole

explanation.surface: A local government area, or else a tree limb that forks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' reads as the word offering an alternative and is the pair of letters that goes inside. A borough is a town with its own council; London is made of thirty-two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A borough is a town or district running its own local government, which makes it literally a division for administration.

clue.text: Champion outside left, pretty grim

indicators.note: To be outside something is to sit round it on both sides, so the longer word opens up to take the short one in.

blocks.note: to champion a cause is to back it
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A star playing outside left and having a wretched afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: Outside left was a winger's position in old football formations, and that phrase is the picture the clue borrows. The two words then split apart: one is the instruction, the other is the letter it moves.
explanation.definitionFit: A black mood or a black day is a thoroughly grim one — the bleak sense of the word rather than the colour.

clue.text: Realistic reproduction of Roman tunic

indicators.note: A reproduction is made over again out of the same material, and here the material is the letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A convincing replica of a tunic worn in ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the museum surface suggests the costume is raw material. The definition uses the sense in 'let's be realistic about this' — seeing things as they are rather than as one would like them.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unromantic takes the practical clear-eyed view, which is what calling a person realistic says about them.

clue.text: Divorcee with attitude: dad’s first to be denounced!

indicators.note: 'First' takes the opening letter of the word beside it and leaves the rest behind.

blocks.note: an ex is a former husband or wife
a pose is an attitude struck for effect
the opening letter of dad

explanation.surface: A divorcee in a temper, and dad is first in line to be named and shamed.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon does the misdirecting, making 'dad's first' look like the opening of a sentence about who gets it worst. The definition is the newspaper sense: a wrongdoer shown up in print.
explanation.definitionFit: To expose someone is to bring their wrongdoing into public view, which is what denouncing them does.

clue.text: Consider bylaws essentially old hat

indicators.note: What is essentially there is there at the core already, sitting inside the words as they are written.

blocks.note: five consecutive letters running from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone weighing up a set of bylaws that have gone out of date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old hat' is both the trap and the definition: as an idiom it means dated, and read straight it is headgear of an earlier age. Nothing has to be assembled — the letters are already lying across the gap between two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A derby is the hard round-crowned hat that Britain calls a bowler, worn in a period long past rather than today.

clue.text: Tree having less on top is topped

blocks.note: a man with less hair on top is balder
the front letter goes, and here that letter is the B

explanation.surface: A tree with a thinning crown having its top cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having less on top' describes a receding hairline rather than a thin crown of branches. Topping a tree genuinely means taking its head off, which is how the sentence stays upright while the wordplay goes elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The alder is a waterside tree of the birch family, common along British riverbanks, so 'Tree' names it by category.

clue.text: Stop druggie being ultimate beneficiary of software

blocks.note: to stop something
someone who takes drugs habitually

explanation.surface: Keeping an addict from being the one who profits from a piece of software.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs on into 3 down, so two short words are clued as a single phrase. 'User' is the pivot between them: the drug sense builds the letters, the computing sense reads them back.
explanation.definitionFit: The end user is the person software is finally written for, as against the people who write, sell or install it.

clue.text: Have a hippie liking for drugs Edward’s taken in

blocks.note: to dig something is to enjoy it, in the slang of the sixties
E is ecstasy and the plural asks for two of them
Ted is the everyday shortening of Edward

explanation.surface: An old hippie's fondness for the drugs young Edward has been swallowing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dig' for enjoy is sixties slang, which is what the word hippie is there to signal. 'Taken in' offers the deceived sense and means absorbed — food or information, swallowed and put to use.
explanation.definitionFit: To digest something is to take it in and absorb it, a meal or a long report alike.

clue.text: Pan’s treasure about to be returned?

definitions.note: Pan is the surname and the answer the forename, so the definition names one half of a famous pair of words by the other.

indicators.note: Something returned comes back the way it went, so those two letters are read right to left.

blocks.note: a treasure of a person is a pet, the favourite of the household
re means about, as at the head of a memo

explanation.surface: A hoard belonging to Pan that is about to be handed back.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark apologises for defining a first name by a surname, and only one boy in fiction carries this one. 'Treasure' is the fond word for a person, not a chest of gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Pan is the boy who never grew up, so 'Pan' points straight at the forename that completes him.

clue.text: Paltry thieves start plundering

indicators.note: 'Start' asks for the letter a word starts with and nothing beyond it.

blocks.note: the letter thieves begins with
to rifle a place is to go through it taking whatever can be carried

explanation.surface: Petty thieves setting about a robbery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paltry thieves' reads as one phrase, and that is where the seam hides: the definition is the first word on its own. Rifling is what a burglar does to a chest of drawers.
explanation.definitionFit: A trifling sum or a trifling objection is a negligible one, which is what paltry says of it.

clue.text: Disputed area’s reported money, pure and simple

indicators.note: Reported speech is heard rather than read, so what follows is spelt the way it sounds.

blocks.note: cash is money, and its sound opens the answer
a mere something is that and nothing more — purely and simply it

explanation.surface: A contested region said to run on money, plain and simple.
explanation.walkthrough: Cashmere the wool takes its name from the region, so the sound being built is one the solver half knows already. 'Pure and simple' is a single phrase doing one job, not two separate words.
explanation.definitionFit: Kashmir is the Himalayan territory claimed by both India and Pakistan, the long-running dispute the definition points at.

clue.text: Cabin aired by working seaman?

definitions.note: The second half describes the word rather than swapping for it: it says who performs the thing and when, which is how the word is normally defined.

blocks.note: a crude one-room hut knocked together out of scrap timber
the song sailors sang to keep time while hauling ropes

explanation.surface: A sailor singing away in his hut.
explanation.walkthrough: Two unrelated words happen to be spelt the same way: one comes from the French chantez, sing, the other probably from a Canadian logger's chantier. The question mark covers the second half being a description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A shanty is a crude hut of scrap timber; a sea shanty is the rhythmic song a crew sang while hauling on a rope.

clue.text: Good to break poor tutor’s rough spirit

indicators.note: Breaking into something forces a way in, so the single letter is driven in among the others.
What is poor is in no fit state, and letters in no fit state need putting into a different order.

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, thrown in with the rest
anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: A bad teacher's coarse temper broken open by a bit of goodness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' is the pivot: the sentence wants a person's nature, the grid wants what is in the bottle. Rotgut is the name for liquor cheap enough to do your insides harm.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotgut is cheap harsh liquor, and spirits of that quality are rough in the most literal way.

clue.text: Inclined to prattle? Try second drink (friendly tip)

indicators.note: The tip of a word is its far end, which means the last letter and no more of it.

blocks.note: to have a go at something is to try it
standard abbreviation
a sip is a small drink
the tip of friendly is the letter at its end

explanation.surface: Offering someone a quick second drink along with a bit of friendly advice.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'friendly tip' looks like the advice on offer and asks for a final letter instead. The question mark marks the definition as a description of a person rather than a one-word synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone gossipy is given to idle chatter about other people, which is exactly being inclined to prattle.

clue.text: Mastermind introduction of baby shower

indicators.note: What introduces a word is the letter that comes on first, before anything else is heard.

blocks.note: the letter baby comes in on
a shower is a short fall of rain

explanation.surface: Organising the opening of a baby shower.
explanation.walkthrough: A baby shower is a party thrown for an expectant mother, and the clue cuts the phrase in half so that the weather word is left on its own. 'Mastermind' is the noun, the brains of an outfit, not the verb the sentence uses.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone the brain of an operation makes them its mastermind, the one whose thinking runs it.

clue.text: Tack produced by supporter at United’s final

indicators.note: The final letter is the one standing at the very end of the word named.

blocks.note: the undergarment whose whole job is support
the last letter of United

explanation.surface: Something knocked together by a fan at United's cup final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'United's final' is a cup tie in the sentence and the closing letter of a word in the wordplay. A brad is the thin nail with almost no head that picture framers use.
explanation.definitionFit: A brad is a slender nail with a barely-there head, which is what a tack is in the carpenter's sense.

clue.text: Crafty assessor of tax, one covered by scheme

indicators.note: To be covered by something is to have it lying over you on either side, so the short piece ends up inside the long one.

blocks.note: to tax someone is to test them, the sense in a taxing question
a plot is a scheme
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A cunning tax inspector, one caught up in a scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crafty' is not sly here: craft means aircraft, and the answer's job is assessing them. 'Tax' hides its other sense, to strain or try, inside a sentence about the Revenue.
explanation.definitionFit: A test pilot flies new aircraft to find out how they behave, so 'crafty assessor' means someone who assesses craft.

clue.text: Kitty gets wind up

indicators.note: In a down entry, up means reading the letters back up the column instead of down it.

blocks.note: to wind is to loop, and LOOP read back up the column gives the answer

explanation.surface: Kitty taking fright.
explanation.walkthrough: To get the wind up is British for taking fright, and the clue's four words invite exactly that reading. The grid wants the other kitty, the common fund on the card table.
explanation.definitionFit: The kitty is the pot everyone pays into, which is what a pool of money is.

clue.text: Plane possibly needs way to ditch wings

indicators.note: Ditching something is throwing it away, so the letters named are dropped and never appear.

blocks.note: a street is a way through a town
the wings of a word are the letters on each flank, here the S and the T

explanation.surface: An aircraft looking for a road to come down on now that its wings have gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ditch' is aviation slang for putting an aircraft down in water, which is what keeps the surface airborne. The plane of the definition is the broad-leaved tree that lines London's streets.
explanation.definitionFit: The plane is one species among many, so 'possibly' marks the definition as an example of the wider family.

clue.text: Virtue of one-time payment made by conquered country?

blocks.note: a is one, as in a hundred meaning one hundred
standard abbreviation
the money a beaten state had to pay its conqueror year by year

explanation.surface: A single payment handed over by a defeated nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One-time' reads as a single occasion and comes apart into two separate letters, hyphen and all. Tribute for enforced payment is the older sense of a word now mostly used for a compliment.
explanation.definitionFit: An attribute is a quality belonging to someone, and virtue carries that same older sense of a quality or merit, as in the virtues of a plan.

clue.text: Cat’s powerless to make sudden leap

indicators.note: Being without power means the letter that stands for power is gone from the word.

blocks.note: to pounce is to make a sudden leap
P is the physics symbol for power, and it is the letter dropped from the front

explanation.surface: A cat with no strength left to spring.
explanation.walkthrough: The ounce is the snow leopard of the high Himalaya, a name out of the old bestiaries that crosswords have kept in circulation. 'Powerless' is the setter's standard way of asking for a P to go.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce is the snow leopard, so 'Cat' names the animal by its family.
